# Introduction to 1 Chronicles

## Part 1: General Introduction

### Outline of the book of 1 Chronicles

1. Genealogies (ancestor lists) leading from Adam to David and Saul
    1. From Adam to the descendants of Isaac’s son Esau (1:1–54)
    2. The descendants of Isaac’s son Israel (2:1–7:40), including David (2:15, 3:1–9)
    3. The genealogy and death of Saul (8:1–40, 9:35–44, 10:1–14)
    4. Israelites who returned from exile in Babylon (9:1–34)
2. The reign of King David (11:1–29:30)
    1. Warriors who supported David (11:1–12:40)
    2. How David became established and made Jerusalem a sacred place (13:1–17:27)
    3. How David and his warriors defeated Israel’s enemies (18:1–20:8)
    4. How David establish worship arrangements for the Israelites (21:1–29:30)

### What is the book of 1 Chronicles about?

The book of 1 Chronicles is the first part of a history of David and his descendants who were kings of Israel and Judah. The book first situates David’s ancestry among all of the descendants of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. It then relates the death of Saul, Israel’s first king, and it tells how David became the next king. It describes David’s military triumphs and his preparations for a temple in Jerusalem. It ends with his death. This history continues through the book of 2 Chronicles, which describes David’s successors up to the time of the Babylonian exile. (The books of Ezra and Nehemiah continue this story further and tell what happened after the return from exile.)

This entire history was compiled and composed after the Judeans returned from exile in Babylon. It is designed to show the restored community that it can still fulfill the purposes that Yahweh has for it as his chosen people. So it begins with a long series of genealogies (ancestor lists) that start with Adam, the first man, and trace the branches of his descendants down through key figures such as Noah, Abraham, Jacob, and Judah. The design is to show how Yahweh chose people in various historical periods to further his purposes. This leads ultimately to David. The book describes at length the special role he had in helping the Israelite community live in peace and safety and become centered on the worship of Yahweh.

The message is one of encouragement for the returned exiles. It may have been difficult for them to think of themselves as a distinctive community. They were still ruled by a foreign emperor, and their cities and their temple were in ruins. But the book stresses that if they will worship Yahweh in the way that he desires, particularly following the arrangements that David established, not only will this restore their special identity, they will also help people from all nations come to have faith in Yahweh.

### Who wrote the book of 1 Chronicles?

The author of 1 Chronicles does not state his name, and he does not provide any personal information about himself. So it is not possible to identify who wrote this book.

### What title should translators use for this book?

Translators can use a traditional title such as “The First Book of Chronicles” or “First Chronicles.” They might also call it by a different title such as “The Ancestry and Story of King David.”

### What kind of writing is the book of 1 Chronicles?

Much of the book of 1 Chronicles consists of historical narratives, that is, stories about things that happened in the past. However, the book also contains many lists. There is also a long section of poetry in 16:8–36. Consider how to represent these forms of writing in a way that your readers will appreciate. There are suggestions later in this introduction for how to represent lists.

### Translating names

This book presents many names of people and places. We recommend that in your translation, you spell them the way they sound in your language. However, if a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the spelling that it uses for some common names if that would be more familiar to your readers. For example, a translation in your region might use the name “Solomon,” and you may choose to use that name rather than spelling it “Shelomoh.”

In many cases, the text indicates whether a person is a man (by identifying him as someone’s father, son, or brother) or a woman (by identifying her as someone’s mother, daughter, sister, or wife). Notes will say when a person is a woman if this is not indicated in the text. Otherwise, translators may assume that the person is a man.

In the same way, the text will typically indicate whether a place name is for a city (“And the name of his city: Dinhabah,” 1:43), a region (“the land of Edom,” 1:43), a mountain (“Mount Seir,” 4:42), a river (“the river of Gozan,” 5:26), and so forth. If your language has its own way of expressing the names of particular kinds of places, you should be able to follow these indications to know how to represent such names.

### Formatting lists

There are many lists in this book. They include the series of genealogies in chapters 1–9, the lists of warriors in chapters 11–12, and the lists of priests and Levites and their responsibilities in later chapters. Some of these lists have summary introductions. Some of them have summary conclusions. Some lists have both, and some have neither. In your translation, format the lists in the way that will help your readers understand them best.

For example, you might indent the entire list and put the verse numbers on the left margin. You might put each element of a list on a separate line, and if there are primary and secondary elements (for example, first the name of a father and then a list of his sons), you might put the secondary element on the line below and indent it more than the primary element. When there is an introduction or conclusion, you might indent it the same as a primary element. You might also use section headings to describe the content of each list. In the first two chapters of the book, the ULT models ways to format these lists in order to make their composition simpler to recognize.

## Part 3: Translation Issues in This Book

### “And it happened”

The author often uses the phrase “And it happened” to introduce a new event in the story or a new development within an event. For example, in 10:8, he introduces the development of the Philistines discovering Saul’s body within the event of the battle of Mount Gilboa by saying, “And it happened on the next day that the Philistines came to strip the slain.” To translate this phrase in its various occurrences, use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event or development.

### “behold”

The author and characters often use the word “behold” to focus their listeners’ attention on what they are about to say. While the word literally means “look,” the speakers do not want their listeners to look at something, but to pay careful attention. For example, in 11:1, the leaders of Israel use the term to call David’s attention to their common ancestry and the right they feel he therefore has to rule the whole nation.

### “brothers”

The author and characters often use the term “brothers” to mean not sons of the same father but members of the same nation, tribe, clan, or extended family. For example, in 12:29, the author speaks of the members of the tribe of Benjamin as the “brothers” of Saul. He means that they were his relatives or kinsmen.

### “to this day”

In 1 Chronicles 4:41, 4:43, 5:26, and 13:11, the author uses the phrase “to this day.” He uses the similar phrase “until now” in 9:18. He is drawing on earlier sources that are referring to the time when they were written. Translators should be aware that “to this day” refers to a time that was already in the past when 1 Chronicles was written centuries ago. They must avoid giving the impression that the expression refers to the present day of their own readers. Notes at each instance will suggest how a translation might express the meaning accurately.

### “in the eyes of”

The author and characters often speak of something being good or bad, or right or wrong, “in the eyes of” someone. For example, the author says in 13:4 that when David proposed to bring the Box of Yahweh to Jerusalem, “the matter was right in the eyes of all of the people.” He means that the people considered this the right thing to do.

### “to the face of”

The expression “to the face of” can have different shades of meaning, depending on the context.
* The author and characters often use the word “face” to represent the presence of a person or group, by association with the way people can see the face of someone who is present. For example, the author says in 11:3 that the Israelites anointed David as king of Israel “to the face of Yahweh.” He means that they did so in the presence of Yahweh.
* The focus may also be on something being in front of or before a person or thing, in space or in time. For example, the author says in 24:2 that Nadab and Abihu died “to the face of” their father Aaron. He means that they died before he did.
* Sometimes the idea of “in front of” has a further association. For example, the author says in 19:16 that when the Arameans gathered a large army, “Shophach, the commander of the army of Hadadezer, was to their faces.” By saying that Shophach was in front of these troops, he means that he was commanding them.
* The focus may also be on the relationship or interaction between people or groups, as in 11:13, where the author says that the Israelite army “fled from the face of the Philistines.” He means that fled from the Philistines as the Philistines opposed and attacked them.

In other contexts, the author or a character may use the word “face,” describing part of a person, in order to represent the whole person. For example, in 17:25, David tells Yahweh that he has found the courage to pray “to your face.” He is using one part of Yahweh, his “face,” to mean all of him. He means that he has prayed to Yahweh himself.

### “into the hand of”/”into your hand”

The author and characters often use the word “hand” to represent power, capability, or control. For example, David says in 21:13, “into the hand of man, let me not fall.” He is saying that he does not want people, specifically enemy nations, to have power over him and harm him.

The word “hand” may also represent possession or conveyance. The author says in 11:3 that the Israelites anointed David as their king “according to the word of Yahweh by the hand of Samuel.” He is referring to a “word” or message that Samuel brought to the Israelites from Yahweh. The word “hand” may also represent agency. The author describes in 16:7 how David arranged for the Israelites to praise Yahweh “by the hand of Asaph and his brothers,” that is, through the agency of Asaph and his fellow Levites, as they sang and played instruments to lead worship. Notes will help distinguish the difference between these shades of meaning when that may not be clear from the context.

In other contexts, the author or a character may use the word “hand,” describing part of a person, in order to represent the whole person. For example, the author says in 6:15 that the Israelites were exiled “by the hand of Nebuchadnezzar.” He is using one part of Nebuchadnezzar, his “hand,” to mean all of him in the act of exiling the Israelites.

### “head”

The author and characters often use the term “head” to mean “leader.” The author says in 11:6 that because Joab led a successful attack against the Jebusites in Jerusalem, “he became the head” of David’s soldiers. He means that he became their leader or commander.

### “house of fathers”

In many places, the author uses the phrase “house of fathers” (or “father’s house”) as a common expression of his culture to describe extended families, comprising three or four generations, led by a man who was the father, grandfather, or great-grandfather of the family members. The household also included servants. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, throughout the book you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning (such as “clans”), or you could state the meaning plainly (as by saying “extended families”).

### “let” and “may”

The ULT uses the English helping verbs “let” and “may” to show that a speaker is expressing a desire that something happen or that someone do something. It uses the verb “let” for more assertive expressions, and it uses the verb “may” for more deferential expressions. For example, when David says in 13:3, “let us bring the Box of our God back to us,” he means, “I want us to bring the Box of our God back to us.” Languages that do not have a volitional form might say, “we ought to bring the Box of our God back to us.” When David tells Solomon in 22:13, “may you not fear,” he is saying what he wants Solomon to do, but he is being more deferential, because he is addressing his own son. Languages that do not have a volitional form might say, “I desire that you not fear,” or they might use an imperative with an indication that it is a polite request, “please do not fear.” Translate this volitional form in the most natural way in your language to indicate that the speaker is expressing what he wishes someone would do.

### “listen”

The author and characters may use the terms “listen” or “hear” to mean complying with what someone has said. For example, the author says in 29:23 that when Solomon became king, “all of Israel listened to him.” He means that the Israelites obeyed Solomon’s commands.

### name of a person representing him and associated or accompanying people

The author and characters often use the name of a person to represent that person and others who are associated with or accompanying that person. For example, in 14:11, when the author says that David struck or defeated the Philistines, he is using David, one person who was involved in this action, to represent everyone who was involved. The text makes clear that it was David and all of his soldiers who did this.

### name of nation, tribe, or city representing its people

The author and characters often use the name of a nation, tribe, or city to represent its people or its army. For example, in 2:7, when the author describes Achar as “the troubler of Israel,” he is using the name of the nation of Israel to mean the people of that nation, the Israelites. (When a nation has the same name as its ancestor, as in this case, this is the same thing as using the name of the ancestor to mean his descendants.)

### “saying”

The author and characters frequently use the term “saying” to introduce a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this term explicitly.

### “shall”

The ULT represents the Hebrew instructional verb form with the English helping verb “shall.” For example, when David asks in 11:19, using the question form for emphasis, “Shall I drink the blood of these men with their lives?” he means “I should not drink” or “I must not drink.” Translate this form with the most natural way in your language for giving instructions.

### “sons of”

The author and characters often speak of “the sons of” a person to mean the nation or tribe that consists of his descendants. For example, in 19:1, he describes Nahash as the king of the “sons of Ammon.” In such contexts, “sons” does not mean first-generation offspring, but later descendants. The author means that Nahash was the king of the Ammonites.

### “strike/struck”

In many places, the author says that soldiers “struck” an opposing army, city, or king as if they had merely hit them. But he means that they attacked those opponents and usually that they defeated them. That is the case 20:1, where the author says that “Joab struck Rabbah.” He means that Joab and the Israelite army defeated and conquered that city. In some contexts, the specific meaning of “struck” is “killed.” The author describes in 20:4 how, in single combat, Sibbecai the Hushathite “struck” the Philistine giant Sippai. He means that he killed him.

### travel descriptions marked for change in elevation (“went up,” “went down”)

In Hebrew, writers and speakers generally indicated whether people were going up to a higher elevation or going down to a lower elevation when they traveled. For example, in 13:6, the author says that David and the Israelites went to Kiriath Jearim “bring up from there the Box of God.” He says “bring up” because Jerusalem, where David wanted to bring the Box, was higher than Kiriath Jearim. If your language does not generally mark travel for change in elevation, you do not need to do that in your translation.

# 1 Chronicles 1 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter begins the series of genealogies (ancestor lists) that begin with Adam, the first man, and trace the line of his descendants ultimately to David. The genealogies in this chapter go as far as the two sons of Isaac, who were Esau and Israel. One principle of these genealogies is that after introducing a key figure (such as Adam, Noah, Abraham, or Israel), they first trace the line that does not lead toward David, and then they trace the line that does.

1. From Adam to Isaac’s sons Esau and Israel (1–34)
    1. From Adam to Noah and his sons (1–4)
    2. The descendants of Noah’s son Japheth (5–7)
    3. The descendants of Noah’s son Ham (8–16)
    4. The descendants of Noah’s son Shem (17–23)
    5. From Shem to Abraham (24–27)
    6. The descendants of Ishmael (28–31)
    7. The descendants of Abraham’s concubine Keturah (32–33)
    8. The descendants of Abraham’s wife Sarah: Isaac and his sons Esau and Israel (34)
2. The descendants of Esau (35–42)
3. The kings and chiefs of the Edomites, Esau’s descendants (43–54)
    1. The kings of Edom (43–51a)
    2. The chiefs of Edom (51b–54)

* The list of descendants from Adam to Noah and his sons (1–4) and the list from Shem to Abraham (24–27) each contain ten names, ending with a key figure and providing further information about that figure. It may be helpful to your readers if you format both of these lists in the same way so that they can see this connection.
* The lists of the descendants of Noah’s sons in 5–7, 8–9, and 17 have primary and secondary elements. So do the lists in verses 28–42.
* The list of the kings of Edom in 43–51a has an introductory summary. The lists of Joktan’s, Ishmael’s, and Keturah’s descendants in verses 20–23, 29–31, and 32–33 have concluding summaries. The list of the chiefs of Edom in 51b–54 has an introductory summary and a concluding summary.

# 1 Chronicles 2 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues the series of genealogies with which this book begins. In the previous chapter, the genealogies traced the line from Adam to Isaac and his two sons Esau and Israel, and it listed the descendants of Esau. Now the book, in chapters 2–7, will list the descendants of Israel. (The book does not list the descendants of two of Israel’s sons, Dan and Zebulun. Interpreters are not sure why it does not list them.) Judah, the ancestor of the tribe of David, is considered the most important of his sons, and so the list begins by describing Judah’s descendants in this chapter.

1. List of the sons of Israel (1–2)
2. From Judah to his great-grandsons, the sons of Hezron (3–9)
3. The descendants of Hezron’s son Ram, including Jesse and his children (10–17)
4. The descendants of Hezron’s son Caleb (18–19)
5. The descendants of Hezron by his wife, the daughter of Makir (20–23)
6. The descendant of Hezron by his wife Abjijah (24)
7. The descendants of Hezron’s son Jerahmeel (25–41)
8. More descendants of Hezron’s son Caleb (42–48)

See the discussion in the introduction to 1 Chronicles of how to format lists so that their composition is simpler to understand. Also see how you formatted the lists in chapter 1 that had various characteristics such as primary and secondary elements, introductory summaries, and concluding summaries. The ULT models ways to format the lists in this chapter.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The name Jabez

In verse 10, Jabez asks God not to act harmfully toward him “so as not to pain me.” The word that the ULT translates as “pain” comes from a root related to the name Jabez. So Jabez is making a play on words with his own name as he prays to God. In this culture, people believed that a person’s name indicated something that was true about him. (In many cases, a person’s name was changed as a result of something he achieved or something that happened to him.) Although verse 9 explains that the mother of Jabez gave him this name because she bore him after a painful labor, he seems to have been concerned that he would have to deal with poverty and difficult circumstances throughout his life. So by praying in this way, he is asking God to reverse the potential implications of his name. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain this in a footnote.

It then repeats the genealogy of Saul from 8:29–38 in order to introduce the story of the Israelite kings that begins with Saul and continues through the rest of this book and through 2 Chronicles.

    3. People from the tribe of Benjamin (7–9)

2. Duties of various Levites (22b–34)
    1. Duties of the gatekeepers (22b–26)
    2. Duties of other Levites (27–34)
3. Genealogy of Saul (35–44)

# 1 Chronicles 10 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter begins the author’s story of the kings of Israel, which continues through the rest of this book and through 2 Chronicles. The author is particularly interested in David and his descendants, but he begins by relating how and why Saul, the first king of Israel, died. He wants to demonstrate that David did not take the throne away from Saul illegitimately. Instead, Yahweh punished Saul for his disobedience, and he chose David as the next king.

1. How Saul died in battle with the Philistines (1–6)
2. The aftermath of the battle (7–12)
3. The sins for which Yahweh replaced Saul with David as king (13–14)

# 1 Chronicles 11 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter begins the author’s account of the reign of David. He is particularly interested in David as the king who, under Yahweh’s inspiration and direction, introduced the worship arrangements that his audience, the community of returned exiles, may now resume in order to maintain the continuity of Israel’s worship. The author wants to show how David had the full support of the Israelite nation and its greatest warriors. So he begins his account of David in this chapter by relating episodes that demonstrate that he had this support.

1. The elders of all Israel anoint David as king (1–3)
2. David and the whole Israelite army conquer Jerusalem (4–9)
3. The great warriors who supported and defended David (11–47)

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Differences in some names between 11:10–47 and 2 Samuel 23:8–39

There are two lists in the Bible of David’s greatest warriors, here in 11:10–47 and in 2 Samuel 23:8–39. There are some differences in the names of the warriors, and there are more warriors listed in this book than in 2 Samuel. Notes will identify each of the differences and, when possible, suggest which book may be presenting the more ordinary form of a name. However, in most cases, there are no Hebrew manuscripts or ancient versions of 2 Samuel that read as 1 Chronicles does, and none of 1 Chronicles read as 2 Samuel does. So we recommend that you do not try to use the same personal and clan names in both books in your translation. You may wish to indicate in a footnote which book more likely preserves the more ordinary form of a name in each instance.

The author is speaking of a whole, **all of Israel**, to mean a part of that whole, representatives of the various Israelite tribes who **gathered to David**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And representatives of the various tribes of Israel]

The tribal representatives are using the term **Behold** to focus David’s attention on what they are about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Listen]

Here, **we are your bone and your flesh** was a common expression that the tribal representatives were using to affirm to David that they were related by descent from a common ancestor. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [we are your blood relatives]

The tribal representatives are using **Both yesterday and the third day** as a common expression of his culture to mean the way things had been previously. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the one leading Israel on military campaigns]

Quote: אַתָּ֨ה תִרְעֶ֤ה אֶת־עַמִּ⁠י֙ אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל וְ⁠אַתָּה֙ תִּהְיֶ֣ה נָגִ֔יד עַ֖ל עַמִּ֥⁠י יִשְׂרָאֵֽל
Note: When Yahweh spoke to David as the representatives describe, he was stating the pronoun **you** separately in both of these instances, even though the verbs translated as **you will shepherd** and **you will become** already included this meaning, to emphasize that none other than David would do these things. If speakers of your language would use explicit pronouns for this purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [You are the one who will shepherd my people Israel, and you are the one who will become the ruler over my people Israel]

Quote: אַתָּ֨ה תִרְעֶ֤ה אֶת־עַמִּ⁠י֙ אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל וְ⁠אַתָּה֙ תִּהְיֶ֣ה נָגִ֔יד עַ֖ל עַמִּ֥⁠י יִשְׂרָאֵֽל
Note: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and it would be good to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation rather than combining them. It may be clearer in your language to connect the phrases with a word other than **and** in order to show that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [You are the one who will shepherd my people Israel; indeed, you are the one who will become the ruler over my people Israel]

Yahweh is speaking as if David would actually **shepherd** the people of Israel, as though they were sheep. This image compares the way a shepherd cares for and guides his sheep to the way a king should care for and lead his people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You are the one who will care for and guide my people Israel]

The author is using **cut … a covenant** as a common expression of his culture to mean “make a covenant.” If this phrase would not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and David made a covenant with them]

Here, the **face** of Yahweh represents his “presence.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in the presence of Yahweh]

Here, **word** represents a message or prophecy. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your language or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [according to the message from Yahweh]

Here, **hand** represents the agency of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [that he had Samuel speak for him]

The author is saying **all** as an overstatement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [And David led a large army of Israelite soldiers]

The author is providing background information to explain to readers that the city they know as **Jerusalem** was known at the time as **Jebus**. In your translation, present this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

The author is not referring to a specific **Jebusite**. He means the Jebusites who lived in this fortified area in Jerusalem. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use expressions that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And the Jebusites]

The author assumes that readers will understand that by **the dwellers of the land**, he means that the Jebusites were among the original inhabitants of the land of Canaan, before the Israelites arrived. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [some of the original inhabitants of Canaan]

The author is providing background information to explain to readers that the fortified area that he calls **Zion** is the same area that they know as **the City of David**. In your translation, present this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

See the discussion in the introduction to 1 Chronicles of how the author may use the term **striking** to mean “defeating” in battle. Alternate translation: [The first one to lead our soldiers to defeat the Jebusites]

The terms **head** and **chief** mean similar things. David was using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [the leader of our army] or [my army commander]
The word **Zeruiah** is the name of a woman, David’s older sister.

See the discussion in the introduction to 1 Chronicles of how people in this culture generally indicated whether people were going up to a higher elevation or going down to a lower elevation when they traveled. (Since Jerusalem was on top of a mountain, Joab needed to go to a higher elevation to lead an attack against it.) If your language does not generally mark travel for change in elevation, you do not need to do that in your translation. Alternate translation: [went] or [led an attack]
See how you translated the term “head” in [5:7](../05/07.md). Alternate translation: [and he became the leader]
The word **Millo** is the name of a place. (It was likely a raised platform or landfill that formed part of Jerusalem’s fortifications.)

Quote: וַ⁠יֵּ֥לֶךְ דָּוִ֖יד הָל֣וֹךְ וְ⁠גָד֑וֹל וַ⁠יהוָ֥ה צְבָא֖וֹת עִמּֽ⁠וֹ
Note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [And since Yahweh of Armies was with him, David went, going and becoming great]

The author is using **went, going and becoming great** as a common expression of his culture to mean “kept becoming greater and greater.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And David kept becoming greater and greater]
See how you translated the similar expression in [9:20](../09/20.md). Alternate translation: [Yahweh of Armies was helping him]
See how you translated the term “head” in [5:7](../05/07.md). Alternate translation: [the leaders]

While this is a reflexive verbal form, the emphasis is not on what these **warriors** did for themselves but on what they did to help David. The idea is that they summoned their own strength on his behalf. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the ones who summoned their strength to help him]

The author is saying **all** as an generalization for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [with the other Israelites]

The author is using the term **word** to represent what Yahweh said by using words. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [according to what Yahweh had said]

See the discussion in the introduction to this chapter of the differences in names between this list of David’s greatest warriors and the one in 2 Samuel 23:8–39. In [2 Samuel 23:8](../2sa/23/08.md), this man may be called Josheb Basshebeth the Tahchemonite, or the text may mean “the Tahchemonite who sat in the chief seat.” Many scholars believe that 1 Chronicles presents the more ordinary forms of his personal and clan names.

The author is speaking as if Jashobeam’s **spear** had actually been asleep and he was **awakening** it. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He aggressively used his spear as a weapon]

The author is using the adjective **Thirty** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase, here and throughout this chapter. It may be natural in some languages for the number to serve as a title or group name, as in the ULT. Alternate translation: [David’s 30 greatest warriors]

The phrase **the Thirty** is a translation of the standard written Hebrew text as we have it today. There is, however, a correction in the margin of the text that Hebrew scribes have recommended. You may want to follow this correction in your translation, or you may want to follow the major translation in your area. Alternate translation: [the officers]

The author is using the adjective **300** as a noun to mean a certain kind of thing, a person, and specifically an enemy soldier. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [300 enemy soldiers]

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. He is using simply the singular term **slain** to describe the state into which Jashobeam put these enemy soldiers. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [whom he slew]

Quote: וְ⁠אַחֲרָ֛י⁠ו אֶלְעָזָ֥ר בֶּן־דּוֹד֖וֹ הָ⁠אֲחוֹחִ֑י ה֖וּא בִּ⁠שְׁלוֹשָׁ֥ה הַ⁠גִּבֹּרִֽים
Note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information that this man was **among the three warriors** before his name. Alternate translation: [And after him among the three warriors was Eleazar the son of Dodo, the son of Ahohi]
In this context, the term **people** means “soldiers.” Alternate translation: [the Israelite soldiers]

Here the phrase **from their face** is a common expression of the culture that means “from in front of.” The sense is that the Israelite soldiers knew that the Philistines were powerfully attacking them and so they no longer wanted to oppose them in battle. Alternate translation: [from the attack of the Philistines]

The pronoun **they** here and in the rest of the verse and the pronoun **themselves** refer to Eleazar and David. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [But Eleazar and David stationed themselves]

The author is describing one event before describing another event that preceded it. If it would be helpful your language, you may wish to relate these events in the order in which they happened. Alternate translation: [and they struck the Philistines, and they delivered it]
See how you translated the term “struck” in [1:46](../01/46.md). Alternate translation: [and they defeated the Philistines]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [And Yahweh powerfully saved the Israelites]

The author is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. The UST models one way to do that.
See how you translated the similar expression in [11:6](../11/06.md). Alternate translation: [went]

The author is using the image of the **head** to mean a leader or chief. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the chief Thirty] or [the leading Thirty]
See how you translated the term “Thirty” in [11:11](../11/1.md). Alternate translation: [David’s 30 greatest warriors]

The author assumes that readers will understand that by **the rock**, he means the cliff in which the **cave of Adullam** was located. He assumes further that readers will know that David hid in that cave to escape from Saul, as [1 Samuel 22:1–22](../1sa/22/01.md) describes. You could indicate these things explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [to help David when he was hiding from Saul in the cave of Adullam, which was in a rocky cliff]

The author is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this.
The author is using the word **camp** to mean the Philistine soldiers who were in this camp. Alternate translation: [And a Philistine army]

Quote: וְ⁠דָוִ֖יד אָ֣ז בַּ⁠מְּצוּדָ֑ה וּ⁠נְצִ֣יב פְּלִשְׁתִּ֔ים אָ֖ז בְּ⁠בֵ֥ית לָֽחֶם
Note: It might seem that saying “then” in both parts of this verse would be extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could say “then” in only one part of the verse, wherever it would be more natural in your language to say that.

Since what David says in the rest of the verse indicates what he **desired**, you do not need to explain that here at the beginning of the verse by saying something such as, “And David desired to have something to drink.”

Quote: מִ֚י יַשְׁקֵ֣⁠נִי מַ֔יִם מִ⁠בּ֥וֹר בֵּֽית־לֶ֖חֶם אֲשֶׁ֥ר בַּ⁠שָּֽׁעַר
Note: David is using the question form to express his strong desire for water from the well. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I wish that someone would give me water from the well of Bethlehem that is at the gate!]

The term for **waters** is always plural in Hebrew. Different languages may need to use a singular form in certain contexts, as the ULT does in many other places and as the UST does here. However, since the Hebrew says **them** in the next verse, the ULT uses a plural form here. If your language would use a plural form in such a context, it would be appropriate to do that in your translation.

The author is using the adjective **three** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [And the three great warriors]

The pouring out of the water was a symbolic action by which David showed that this water, obtained at great risk by his men, was too precious to drink, and it deserved to be offered to Yahweh instead. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [and he poured it out on the ground instead as an offering to Yahweh]

David is using a common expression of his culture to express his horror at the idea he describes. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [God forbid that I should do this!]

See the discussion in the introduction to 1 Chronicles of the Hebrew instructional form that the ULT represents with the English helping verb “shall.” Alternate translation: [Should I drink the blood of these men with their lives]

David is using the question form to emphasize that he should not do what he describes. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I should certainly not drink the blood of these men with their lives!]

David is using **with their lives** as a common expression of his culture to mean “who risked their lives.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the blood of these men who risked their lives]

David is speaking as if the water that the men brought were actually their **blood**. He means that the water represents the danger into which these men put their lives to get it for him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [this water that I am pouring out, since the blood of these men could just as easily have been poured out when they risked their lives to get it]
Here the word **For** introduces not a reason but an explanation. Alternate translation: [After all,]

The pronoun **them** refers to the “waters” the men got for David (v. 18). It may be more natural in some languages to use a singular pronoun. Alternate translation: [they brought it with their lives] or [they risked their lives to get it for me]

The author is offering a summary of the stories he has just related. This signals the end of this section about these **three warriors**. Use a natural way in your language to offer a summary that concludes a section. Alternate translation: [Those are some of the things that David’s three mighty warriors did for him] or [So ends the account of what these three warriors did]

The author seems to be describing two different groups of three warriors. In order to distinguish between them, the ULT treats the word **Three** as a title (uppercase) when it describes the great warriors of the first rank, Jashobeam ([11:11](../11/11.md)), Eleazar ([11:12](../11/12.md)), and an unnamed third warrior. It treats the word **three** as a description (lowercase) when it describes the great warriors of the second rank, Abishai (here and in the next verse), Benaiah ([11:22–25](../11/22.md)), and another unnamed warrior. Your language may have a convention of its own that you could use to distinguish between these groups, or you could use descriptive phrases, as the UST does.

The author is stating the pronoun **he** separately, even though the verb translated as **he was** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize the identify of **Abishai** as the man who was the **head** of these warriors. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [he was the one who was the head of the three]

The author is using the image of the **head** to represent a leader or commander. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the commander of]
See how you translated the similar expression in [11:11](../11/11.md). Alternate translation: [and he aggressively used his spear as a weapon]
See how you translated the same expression in [11:11](../11/11.md). Alternate translation: [300 enemy soldiers, whom he slew]

Here, **name** represents reputation or honor. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language, here and in verse 24. Alternate translation: [And he had as great a reputation as the Three]

The author is using the adjectives **three** and **second** as nouns. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate these adjective with equivalent phrases. Alternate translation: [From the three warriors in the second rank, he was honored]

The author is using the term **From** to introduce a comparison. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. You could also use plain language. Alternate translation: [Of the three warriors in the second rank, he was the most honored]

The expression **was honored** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [People honored him the most of the three warriors in the second rank] or [People honored him the most of the next three of David’s greatest warriors]

If your language would not represent a number in a form such as **second**, you could represent this number in a form that your language would use, or you could use an equivalent expression. Alternate translation: [in rank two] or [next greatest warriors]

Here, **come to** represents joining or achieving the same level of status as the Three. The verse means that although Abishai was a great warrior and was highly honored, he did not achieve membership in or equal status with the Three. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly, here and in verse 25. Alternate translation: [But he did not join the ranks of the Three] or [But he did achieve the same exploits and reputation as the Three]

If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information that Benaiah was **from Kabzeel** with the information that he was the **son of Jehoiada**. Alternate translation: [Benaiah, the son of Jehoiada, from Kabzeel, was a son of a man of valor, great of deeds]

In certain contexts, biblical authors and characters use the expression **son of** to indicate that a person has the characteristic of something. In this case, the author is saying that Benaiah has the characteristic of **valor**. Alternate translation: [was characterized by being a man of valor]

The author is using the possessive form to indicate that the **deeds** Benaiah did were **great**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [who did great deeds]

The author is stating the pronoun **he** separately in each of these instances, even though the verbs translated as **he struck** and **he went down** already include this meaning. He is doing that to confirm Benaiah’s exclusive personal role in accomplishing these feats. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for this same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing that the author is confirming Benaiah’s exclusive personal role. It may not be necessary to represent the separately stated pronoun explicitly. Alternate translation: [He single-handedly struck … And he went down alone]
See how you translated the term “struck” in [4:43](../04/43.md). Alternate translation: [he killed … and killed]

Interpreters do not understand exactly what the term **Ariel** means. However, many interpreters believe that it may be describing warrior champions as lion-like, that is, strong and fierce. Alternate translation: [two mighty champions of Moab] or [two fierce warrior heroes of Moab]

While the term **Ariel** is singular in the original, since the author is referring to **two** such people, it may be more natural in your language to use a plural form. Alternate translation: [Ariels]
See how you translated the similar expressions in [11:22](../11/22.md). Alternate translation: [And he was the one who killed]

he author is using **a man of measure** as a common expression of his culture to mean a giant. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a giant]
The author is using the phrase **five by the cubit** to express height in a way characteristic of his culture. Alternate translation: [five cubits tall]

A **cubit** was an ancient unit of measurement corresponding to the distance between an average person’s elbow and middle fingertip, or about 46 centimeters or 18 inches. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could express this man’s height in modern measurements, either in the text or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [seven and a half feet tall]

The point of this comparison is that just as a weaver’s **beam** is very thick and strong, so was the shaft of this man’s **spear**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [that was thick and strong, like a weaver’s beam]

The author seems to mean that Benaiah **went down** from the Israelite battle lines on a safe height, and he went into a valley to fight this **man of Egypt** in single combat between the battle lines. Alternate translation: [and he went into a valley to fight him in single combat]

The author is offering a summary of the stories he has just related. This signals the approaching end of this section about **Benaiah, the son of Jehoiada**. Use a natural way in your language to offer a summary that concludes a section. Alternate translation: [Those are some of the things that Benaiah, the son of Jehoiada, did as one of David’s warriors] or [So ends the account of Benaiah, the son of Jehoiada]

The author is repeating the term **him** for emphasis. It might seem that this expression contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you can shorten it. Alternate translation: [behold him, being honored]

The expression **behold him** is one that people of this culture would commonly use to mean that someone was about to do something, but in this context, the participle form **being honored** seems to indicate ongoing rather than imminent action. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he was continually honored]

The expression **being honored** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [people continually honored him]

The author is speaking as if David had put Benaiah **over**, or physically above, his **bodyguard**. He means that David put Benaiah in charge of his bodyguard, that is, he made him the commander of those soldiers. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And David made him the commander of his bodyguard]
See how you translated the similar expression in [7:5](../07/05.md). Alternate translation: [And the very great warriors]

The names **Shammoth**, **Harorite**, and **Pelonite** are variant spellings of “Shammah,” “Harodite,” and “Paltite,” which are found in [2 Samuel 23:35–36](../2sa/23/35.md). Many scholars believe that 2 Samuel preserves the more ordinary spellings of these names. The name “Elika the Harodite” appears between the names of these two men in 2 Samuel. See the discussion in the introduction to this chapter of the differences between the names of warriors in this book and in 2 Samuel.

[2 Samuel 23:27](../2sa/23/27.md) reads “Mebunnai” rather than **Sibbecai**. Most scholars consider Sibbecai to be the correct form of the name. [2 Samuel 23:28](../2sa/23/28.md) reads “Zalmon” rather than **Ilai**. Most scholars consider Zalmon to be the more complete form of the name.
[2 Samuel 23:29](../2sa/23/29.md) reads “Heleb” rather than **Heled**. Most scholars consider Heled to be the correct form of the name.

[2 Samuel 23:30](../2sa/23/30.md) reads “Hiddai” rather than **Hurai**. Most scholars consider Heled to be the correct form of the name. [2 Samuel 23:31](../2sa/23/31.md) reads “Abi Albon” rather than **Abiel**. Abiel could be a shorter form of Abi Albon.
[2 Samuel 23:31](../2sa/23/31.md) reads “Barhumite” rather than **Baharumite**. Most scholars consider Baharumite to be the more original form and Barhumite to be a variant spelling.

[2 Samuel 23:32](../2sa/23/32.md) reads “the sons of Jashen” rather than **the sons of Hashem the Gizonite**. Scholars are uncertain which book preserves a more original reading. Some suggest that the texts should be read Beni Hashem and Beni Jashen and that both are developments of this man’s original name.

[2 Samuel 23:32–33](../2sa/23/32.md) reads “Jonathan; Shammah the Hararite” rather than **Jonathan, the son of Shagee, the Hararite**. Scholars suggest that the phrase “the son of” may have dropped out of 2 Samuel and that “Shammah” is more likely the original form, referring back to the man who is called “Shammoth” here in [11:27](../11/27.md) but “Shammah” in [2 Samuel 23:35–36](../2sa/23/35.md).

[2 Samuel 23:34](../2sa/23/34.md) reads “Eliphelet, the son of Ahasbai, the son of the Maacathite” rather than the way the text reads here. Eliphal seems to be a shortened form of Eliphelet. It is unclear whether Ur or Ahasbai is closer to the original form of this name. It is possible that the parallel in 2 Samuel should be read as describing two men: “Eliphelet, the son of Ahasbai; the son of the Maacathite.” The “son of the Maacathite” would then mean **Hepher the Mecherathite**, with Maacathite being the more ordinary spelling of the clan name.
[2 Samuel 23:33](../2sa/23/33.md) reads “Sharar” rather than **Sachar**. Most scholars consider Sachar to be the more original form.

[2 Samuel 23:34](../2sa/23/34.md) reads “Eliam, the son of Ahithophel the Gilonite” rather than **Ahijah the Pelonite**. It is possible that Ahijah, “Yah is brother,” is a variant of Eliam, “God is kinsman,” and that the author is saying Pelonite, a reference to an indefinite person (“so-and-so”), so as not to name Ahithophel the Gilonite, the counselor of David who betrayed him. In that case, 2 Samuel would preserve the more original reading.

[2 Samuel 23:35](../2sa/23/35.md) reads “Paarai the Arbite” rather than **Naarai, the son of Ezbai**. It is possible that Naarai and Paarai are variations of the same original name and that 1 Chronicles names this man’s father while 2 Samuel names his clan.

[2 Samuel 23:36](../2sa/23/36.md) reads “Igal, the son of Nathan from Zobah; Bani the Gadite” rather than the way the text reads here. Scholars suggest that Joel is a simplified form of Igal, that Mibhar is an abbreviated form of “from Zobah,” and that Hagri is an abbreviated form of “the Gadite.” This suggests that the reading in 2 Samuel preserves the more original forms. It remains unclear whether Joel was the “son” or **brother** of **Nathan**.

From here to the end of the chapter, the author presents names that are not on the corresponding list in 2 Samuel 23:8–39. You should include all of these names in your translation, as these men were among David’s greatest warriors. The number Thirty (verse 11) is a round, symbolic number, and the Bible recognizes and honors a large number of warriors than that. (The parallel passage says “in all, 37” in [2 Samuel 23:39](../2sa/23/39.md).)

# 1 Chronicles 12 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues the author’s account of the beginnings of the reign of David. To show further how David had the full support of the Israelite nation and its greatest warriors, the author describes how warriors joined David at various points even before he became king and how representatives from throughout Israel came to Hebron to make him their king.

1. Warriors who came to David while he was in the stronghold in the wilderness (1–18)
    1. Introduction (1)
    2. Warriors from the tribe of Benjamin (2–7)
    3. Warriors from the tribe of Gad (8–15)

# 1 Chronicles 13 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues the author’s account of the beginnings of the reign of David. To show how David sincerely wanted to honor Yahweh, the author describes in this chapter how David attempted to bring his sacred Box to Jerusalem, his new capital. This first attempt ended tragically with the death of one of the men transporting the Box. But as chapter 15 shows, David learned from this experience that Yahweh must be honored in the ways that he has specified, and this became a principle that David followed and established for future generations of Israelites.

1. David assembles Israel’s leaders to agree to bring the Box to Jerusalem (1–4)
2. A great crowd of Israelites begins to transfer the Box (5–8)
3. This attempt ends in tragedy (9–14)

# 1 Chronicles 15 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues the author’s account of the reign of David. It describes how David realized that the Israelites should have transported the Box of Yahweh to Jerusalem by following the instructions in the law of Moses that the Levites were to carry it on poles. The author describes how the Israelites successfully brought the Box to Jerusalem that way. He also describes the specific arrangements that David and the Levites made for worship on this occasion. These are important for the author to describe because he is particularly interested in David as the king who, under Yahweh’s inspiration and direction, introduced the worship arrangements that his audience, the community of returned exiles, may now resume in order to maintain the continuity of Israel’s worship.

1. David prepares to bring the Box to Jerusalem (1–3)
2. A list of the Levites who assembled for this occasion (4–10)
3. David’s instructions to the priests and Levites (11–15)
4. The arrangements for transporting the Box with music and singing (16–24)
5. The procession of the Box from Obed Edom’s house to Jerusalem (25–29)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Why did Michal disdain David for dancing and celebrating?

The author says in 15:29 that as the Israelites were bringing the Box of Yahweh to Jerusalem, David’s wife Michal “saw King David dancing and celebrating, and she despised him in her heart.” The author does not explain directly why Michal disdained David for doing this. However, he does give a hint in 15:27 when he says that “David was clothed in a robe of fine linen” and “an ephod of linen was on David.” The parallel passage in 2 Samuel 6:14–23 indicates that at some point, probably because he became too warm from dancing, David took off the robe and wore only the ephod. This passage also indicates that, for one thing, Michal felt that this was an inappropriate way for a king to dress. But the author of this book, by not saying that this was the specific reason why Michal disapproved, leaves open the additional possibility that Michal disapproved of David “dancing and celebrating” to honor Yahweh. [1 Samuel 19:13](../1sa/19/13.md) indicates that Michal had an idol in her home, and it is possible that Michal was not a sincere worshiper of Yahweh. To leave both possibilities similarly open in your translation, we recommend that you not suggest a specific reason why Michal disdained David, either in the text or in a footnote.

# 1 Chronicles 16 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues the author’s account of the reign of David. It continues the story of how the Israelites successfully brought the Box of Yahweh to Jerusalem. It includes the words to a song that David composed for the Levites to perform on this occasion. It concludes by describing how David arranged for Levites to offer worship continually to Yahweh in front of the Box in Jerusalem and at Gibeon, where the tabernacle (the tent that was the former location of the Box) remained.

1. The celebration of the Box arriving in Jerusalem (1–6)
2. David’s song of praise (7–36)
3. Worship arrangements for Jerusalem and Gibeon (37–42)
4. Conclusion (43)

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetic song in 16:8–36.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Parallels in the Psalms to the song in 16:8–36

Portions of the song that David wrote for the occasion of bringing the Box to Jerusalem constitute all or part of three psalms in the book of Psalms. It seems that those portions were later adapted for use in worship in the temple in the form of these psalms. If you have already translated those psalms, this will help you translate the song here. These are the parallels:
16:8-22 and Psalm 105:1-15
16:23-33 and Psalm 96:1-13
16:34 and Psalm 106:1
16:35-36 and Psalm 106:47-48

### Does 16:38 describe two different men named Obed Edom?

It is possible that 16:38 is describing two different men named Obed Edom and distinguishing between the two by specifying that the second was “the son of Jeduthun.” The first Obed Edom seems to be the one mentioned with Jeiel in 15:18, 15:21, and 16:5. Given how commonly these two are paired, it seems possible that the name “Jeiel” has dropped out of 16:38, which would explain why the author says “their brothers” rather than “his brothers.” The second Obed Edom seems to be the one mentioned in 15:24. It’s possible that Hosah and Jehiah are variant spellings of the same person’s name. It is unclear whether either of these men named Obed Edom is identical with the man by that name described in 13:13–14, in whose house the Box of Yahweh remained for some time. The author describes him as a “Gittite,” but that does not necessarily mean that he was a Philistine from the city of Gath who therefore could not serve in the temple area. This man could have been a Levite who from the Levitical city of Gath-Rimmon, or one who resided in Gath for a time. In either of those cases, he could have been a Levite who was eligible to sing in front of the Box, like the first Obed Edom in 16:38, or to be a gatekeeper, like the second Obed Edom in that verse. Notes address some translation issues related to this question.

In verses 37–42, the author describes the arrangements David made for perpetual worship at Israel’s holy sites. He begins by saying “And he left” to introduce people whom David stationed in various positions and roles, and then he names those people: Asaph and his relatives (37), Obed Edom and his relatives (38a), Obed Edom and Hosah (38b), Zadok and the priests (39–40), and Heman and Jeduthun (41–42). It may be natural in your language to divide this long sentence into several shorter sentences describing each of these groups of people. The UST models one way to do that.

# 1 Chronicles 17 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues the author’s account of the reign of David. It describes how he wanted to build a temple (a “house”) for Yahweh, but Yahweh told him that he would build a dynasty (a “house”) for David by having his descendants succeed him as king.

1. David tells Nathan he wants to build a temple for Yahweh (1–3)
2. Yahweh gives Nathan a message for David (4–15)
3. David prays to Yahweh in response to this message (16–27)

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Multiple levels of quotation in Yahweh’s message to Nathan

Yahweh speaks a message to the prophet Nathan in 4–14. Within this message, there are second-level, third-level, and fourth-level quotations. The entire message is something that Yahweh said and that the author is quoting, so it is a first-level quotation. Within it, Yahweh tells Nathan what he should say, so that is a quotation within a quotation, or a second-level quotation. Yahweh tells Nathan specifically that he should tell David that he has said something, and what he has said is a third-level quotation. Within it, in verse 6, there is a further direct quotation, which is a fourth-level one. Your language may use quotation marks or some other punctuation or convention to indicate various levels of quotation. The ULT models one way to do that. You could also translate the whole message in such a way that there are not quotations within quotations. The UST models one way to do that.

### David referring to himself in the third person

As David responds to the message that Yahweh sent him through the prophet Nathan, he often speaks of himself in the third person as “your servant” to show humility. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in a humble form in the first person throughout these verses. Notes to several verses suggest ways to do that.
The author is using the words **And it happened** to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.

# 1 Chronicles 18 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues the author’s account of the reign of David. It describes how he defeated the enemy nations that surrounded Israel and took great plunder from them, bringing safety and prosperity to the Israelites. It then gives some details of David’s government administration.

### “to establish his hand at the River of Euphrates”

In [18:3](../18/03.md), the author says that Hadadezer, the ruler of the Aramean kingdom of Zobah Hamath, “went to establish his hand at the River.” Interpreters understand this expression in two main ways. (1) It could mean that Hadadezer led his army against the Israelites in order to ensure that he continued to control his own territory. The kingdom of Zobah lay between the Euphrates River on the east and Israel on the west. Hadadezer may have seen how David had conquered and subdued the Philistines and Moabites, and he may have launched a pre-emptive attack to keep David from conquering him as well. The author may be saying that Hadadezer felt that his authority and control over his territory (his “hand”) had been diminished by David’s military successes against other nations, and so he marched his army out to “establish” control of this area. If you follow this interpretation, you might say in your translation that Hadadezer went out “to assert his control over his territory, from its border with Israel all the way to the Euphrates River.” (2) The expression could also mean that Hadadezer built a monument to himself at the Euphrates River, asserting his control over the territory west of the river, and that he led his army out to set up the monument in order to assert that control. The term “hand” means “monument” in [1 Samuel 15:12](../../1sa/15/12.md), and that could also be the meaning here. However, in this interpretation Hadadezer and his army would have been marching away from Israel and would not necessarily have come into conflict with David. The further implication would have to be that David learned of this action by a hostile king to assert control over his territory, and so he led the Israelite army against him to subdue him. If you follow this interpretation, you might say in your translation that Hadadezer went “to set up a monument to himself at the Euphrates River.”

# 1 Chronicles 19 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues the author’s account of the reign of David. It describes how David tried to express sympathy to the new king of the Ammonites for the death of his father but was instead insulted and rebuffed. It describes how the Ammonites, knowing they had offended David, hired Aramean mercenaries to help them fight Israel and how Joab and his brother Abishai, David’s generals, defeated those armies. Finally, it describes how the Arameans gathered an even larger army and how David led the entire army of Israel to defeat them.

1. Hanun humiliates David’s messengers (1–5)
2. The Ammonites hire mercenaries, but Joab and Abishai defeat them (6–15)
3. The Ammonites gather a larger army, but David defeats them (16–19)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Why did Hanun shave half of the beards of David’s messengers and cut their garments in the middle?

In [10:4](../10/04.md), to insult David’s messengers, the Ammonite king, Hanun, has his servants shave off half of their beards and cut off half of their robes. In just about any context, these actions would have made the men look foolish and exposed them to shame and embarrassment. But in this culture, there may have been a further significance. In this culture, men wore beards, while women did not have them. By leaving the messengers with half-beards, Hanun was symbolically making them neither men nor women. Humans wear clothes, while animals do not. By leaving the messengers with half-robes, Hanun was symbolically making them neither human nor animal. So this was a way of making the messengers symbolically non-existent. Since they represented David personally, it was a way of insulting David by telling him, “You are nothing.” The author of this book does not explain the significance of this action, since his readers would already have understood it. But if it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain it in a footnote.

# 1 Chronicles 21 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues the author’s account of the reign of David. It describes how David ordered Joab and his army commanders to count how many Israelite men were able to fight in the army. It then describes how Yahweh punished the Israelites with a plague for doing that. But the chapter then describes how Yahweh had mercy on the Israelites and stopped the plague before it had killed the people of Jerusalem. David pleaded for them and offered sacrifices that Yahweh accepted.

1. David orders a census of the Israelite fighting men (1–6)
2. Yahweh punishes this sin with a plague (7–14)
3. David intercedes for the people by praying and offering sacrifices (15–27)
4. How the place where he did that became the temple site (28–30)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Why did Joab not count the men from the tribes of Benjamin and Levi?

The author says in 21:6 that Joab did not count the men from the tribes of Benjamin and Levi who were able to serve in the army. The reason he gives is that “the word of the king was abhorrent to Joab,” that is, Joab felt that David had commanded him to do a bad thing. So Joab did not want to do anything worse than he had to. Since the Levites, according to the law of Moses [Numbers 1:47–52](../num/01/47.md), were exempt from military service, Joab did not count them. You may wish to indicate that in a footnote to your translation. Interpreters have suggested a variety of explanations for why Joab also did not count the men from the tribe of Benjamin. One plausible suggestion is that Joab did not want to provoke any conflict between David and the tribe of the former king, Saul. However, since this is less certain, we recommend that you not indicate a reason for this.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Multiple levels of quotation in Yahweh’s message to Gad

Yahweh speaks a message to the prophet Nathan in verse 10. Within this message, there are second-level and third-level quotations. The entire message is something that Yahweh said and that the author is quoting, so it is a first-level quotation. Within it, Yahweh tells Nathan what he should say, so that is a quotation within a quotation, or a second-level quotation. Yahweh tells Nathan specifically that he should tell David that he has said something, and what he has said is a third-level quotation. Your language may use quotation marks or some other punctuation or convention to indicate various levels of quotation. The ULT models one way to do that. You could also translate the whole message in such a way that there are not quotations within quotations. The UST models one way to do that.

Many interpreters of the book of Job identify this character with Satan, the devil, and many interpreters believe that the author is describing that same figure here. # 1 Chronicles 22 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues the author’s account of the reign of David. It begins a section, which comprises the rest of the book, that describes how David established arrangements for the worship of the Israelites. This chapter describes how David made preparations and collected materials for his son Solomon to build a temple for Yahweh.

1. Conclusion to the story of the census and the plague (1)
2. David’s preparations for the temple (2–5)
3. David’s instructions to Solomon (6–16)
4. David’s instructions to the leaders of Israel (17–19)

The first verse of this chapter belongs with the material in the preceding chapter. (The chapter divisions in the Bible were added many centuries after the biblical books were written. In some cases they do not accurately reflect the structure and content of those books.) It may be possible for you to indicate this through formatting. For example, if you are including section headings in your translation, you could put the section heading describing David’s preparations for the temple after verse 1, as some versions do.

The author is concluding the story of the census, the plague, and David’s intercession for the Israelites by quoting something that David said at the end of this story. (What he said indicated an important future result of these events, which the author describes in the following chapters.) Use a natural way in your language to conclude a story. Alternate translation: [As a result of everything that had happened, David said]

David is speaking of the temple he wants the Israelites to build for Yahweh as if it were actually going to be a physical **house** in which Yahweh would live. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly, here and throughout this chapter. Alternate translation: [it will be the temple of Yahweh]

The author does not mean that David prepared this **bronze** without weighing any of it. He means that in the end, there was too much to weigh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. The UST models one way to do that.

# 1 Chronicles 23 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues the final section the book, which describes how David established arrangements for the worship of the Israelites. It relates how David organized the Levites according to their clans to perform various duties related to worship at the temple.

1. David and the Israelite leaders count the Levites (1–5)
2. The divisions that David created from the Levite clans (6–24)
    1. Introduction (6)
    2. Descendants of Gershon (7–11)
    3. Descendants of Kohath (12–20)
    4. Descendants of Merari (21–23)
    5. Conclusion (24)
3. The duties of the Levites (25–32)

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### The extent of the quotation from David that begins in verse 25

Some interpreters believe that verses 28–32 are a continuation of the quotation from David in verses 25–26. They consider verse 27 to be an explanatory aside from the author. Some versions of the Bible reflect this interpretation. If you decide to follow it in your translation, you might present verses 25–32 as follows.

23:25 For David said, “Yahweh, the God of Israel, has given rest to his people. And he dwells in Jerusalem to forever.
23:26 And also for the Levites, {it is} not to carry the tabernacle and all of its vessels for its service”—
23:27 so by the last words of David they were counting the sons of Levi from sons of 20 years and to above—
23:28 “for their service is at the hand of the sons of Aaron for the service of the house of Yahweh, over the courts and over the chambers and over the purifying of all of the holy and the work of the service of the house of God
23:29 and for the bread of the arrangement and for the fine flour for the offering and for the wafers of unleavened bread and for the pan and for the mixing and for every measure and size
23:30 and to stand, by morning by morning, to thank and to praise Yahweh, and thus in the evening,
23:31 and for every offering {of} burnt offerings to Yahweh on the Sabbaths, at the new moons, and at the annual festivals by number according to the regulation about them continually to the face of Yahweh,
23:32 and they keep the keeping of the tent of meeting and the keeping of the holy place and the keeping of the sons of Aaron, their brothers, for the service of the house of Yahweh.”

You could also create a verse bridge for verses 27–32 and put the content of verse 27 after verse 32, after the end of the quotation from David.
