The author is using the term **For** to introduce the reason why the Israelites counted Levites who were at least 20 years old, after originally planning to count those who were at least 30 years old. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [They counted Levites who were at least 20 years old because]

The author is using the term **words** to represent what David commanded by using words. He would mean not that these were the very **last** commands that David gave but that they were commands he gave near the end of his life and reign. Alternate translation: [in obedience to what David commanded near the end of his life]
Here, **sons** means “descendants.” Alternate translation: [the descendants of Levi] or [the Levites]

Some interpreters believe that verses 28–32 are a continuation of the quotation of David in verses 25–26, with verse 27 being an explanatory aside from the author. Some versions of the Bible reflect this interpretation. See the discussion in the introduction to this chapter of how you might present verses 25–32 if you decide to follow this interpretation in your translation.

If verses 28–32 are not a continuation of the quotation of David, then the word **For** would introduce the reason why so many Levites were needed that the count was expanded to include those who were at least 20 years old. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [The reason why so many Levites were needed was that]

Here, **at the hand of** represents “next to.” The idea is that the Levites worked alongside the priests as their assistants. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [they worked next to the sons of Aaron] or [they served as assistants to the sons of Aaron]

The author is describing the priests by reference to the way they were **sons** or descendants of Aaron. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers, here and in verse 32. Alternate translation: [the priests]

The author is speaking as if the Levites were actually **over** or on top of these things. He means that they were responsible for them If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [with responsibility for the courts and the chambers and the purifying of]

The author is using the adjective **holy** as a noun to mean a certain kind of thing. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase, here and in verse 32. Alternate translation: [all of the holy implements]

Since the author has already specified at the start of the verse that the Levites were responsible for this, here he appears to mean that the Levites were responsible for any other necessary aspects of this work that he has not listed. Alternate translation: [and for anything else that was required for the work of the service of the God’s temple]

The author is using a representative **pan** in which the Levites would have baked the **bread of the arrangement** and the **wafers of unleavened bread** to mean the act of baking itself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and for baking them]

Quote: בַּ⁠בֹּ֣קֶר בַּ⁠בֹּ֔קֶר לְ⁠הֹד֥וֹת וּ⁠לְ⁠הַלֵּ֖ל לַ⁠יהוָ֑ה וְ⁠כֵ֖ן לָ⁠עָֽרֶב
Note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information that the Levites sang to Yahweh in the **evening** with the information that they did so in the **morning**. Alternate translation: [by morning, by morning, and thus in the evening, to thank and to praise Yahweh] or [every morning and every evening to thank and to praise Yahweh]

The author is using **by morning, by morning** as a common expression of his culture to mean “every morning.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [morning after morning] or [every morning]

Quote: וּ⁠לְ⁠כֹ֨ל הַעֲל֤וֹת עֹלוֹת֙ לַ⁠יהוָ֔ה לַ⁠שַּׁבָּת֔וֹת לֶ⁠חֳדָשִׁ֖ים וְ⁠לַ⁠מֹּעֲדִ֑ים בְּ⁠מִסְפָּ֨ר
Note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information that the Levites were responsible for preparing the right **number** of animals with the information that these were for **burnt offerings**. Alternate translation: [and for every offering of burnt offerings by number to Yahweh on the Sabbaths, at the new moons, and at the annual festivals] or [and for the right number of burnt offerings for every offering to Yahweh on the Sabbaths, at the new moons, and at the annual festivals]

Here, Yahweh’s **face** represents his presence. Since Yahweh was considered to be especially present at his temple, this could be a reference to the temple area. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in Yahweh’s presence] or [at Yahweh’s temple]

Quote: וְ⁠שָׁמְר֞וּ אֶת־מִשְׁמֶ֣רֶת אֹֽהֶל־מוֹעֵ֗ד וְ⁠אֵת֙ מִשְׁמֶ֣רֶת הַ⁠קֹּ֔דֶשׁ וּ⁠מִשְׁמֶ֕רֶת בְּנֵ֥י אַהֲרֹ֖ן
Note: The author is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [And they cared for the tent of meeting and for the holy and for the sons of Aaron]

The author is speaking of the priests as if they were actual **brothers** of the Levites. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [their kinsmen]

# 1 Chronicles 24 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues the final section the book, which describes how David established arrangements for the worship of the Israelites. It relates how David and the Israelite leaders assigned the priests to a rotating schedule of duty at the temple. It also relates how they assigned certain Levites to assist the priests.

1. How David and the leaders assigned the priests to their schedule (1–6)
2. The schedule of duty for the priests (7–19)
3. The Levite clans that were assigned to assist the priests (20–31)

In this instance and in most of this chapter, the author is using the term **sons** to mean “descendants,” as in [23:28](../23/28.md). However, in the second instance in this verse, the term **sons** is literal. Alternate translation: [And for the descendants of Aaron]

The author is using the expression **to the face of** to mean “before” or “previous to.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [before their father did]

Quote: וַ⁠יֶּֽחָלְקֵ֣⁠ם דָּוִ֔יד וְ⁠צָדוֹק֙ מִן־בְּנֵ֣י אֶלְעָזָ֔ר וַ⁠אֲחִימֶ֖לֶךְ מִן־בְּנֵ֣י אִיתָמָ֑ר
Note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put all the information together about who **divided** the priests into divisions. Alternate translation: [And David and Zadok from the sons of Eleazar and Ahimelech from the sons of Ithamar divided them]
The pronoun **them** refers back to “the sons of Aaron” (the priests) in verse 1. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And David divided the priests]

The author is not referring to a specific **Thing**. He means Things in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [according to their appointments in their service] or [according to the duties to which they were appointed]

The author is using the term **found** in a way characteristic of his language and culture to mean that these **sons of Eleazar** could be found, that is, they were there. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And there were more descendants of Eleazar]
See how you translated the term “head” in [23:8](../23/08.md). Alternate translation: [who were clan leaders]

The author is not referring to a specific **house**. He means the houses of fathers (or clans) of the descendants of Ithamar in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [for the houses of their fathers]

Quote: וַ⁠יַּחְלְק֥וּ⁠ם בְּ⁠גוֹרָל֖וֹת אֵ֣לֶּה עִם־אֵ֑לֶּה כִּי־הָי֤וּ שָֽׂרֵי־קֹ֨דֶשׁ֙ וְ⁠שָׂרֵ֣י הָ⁠אֱלֹהִ֔ים מִ⁠בְּנֵ֥י אֶלְעָזָ֖ר וּ⁠בִ⁠בְנֵ֥י אִיתָמָֽר
Note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [And since officials of the holy place and officials of God were from the sons of Eleazar and among the sons of Ithamar, they divided them by lots, these with these]

The author is using **these with these** as a common expression of his culture to mean that the Israelite leaders drew lots from a collection that included the names of the clans of the descendants of both Elezar and Ithamar. The idea is that the lots were drawn impartially, without giving an advantage to the descendants of either man. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [selecting from the descendants of both men together] or [impartially]

The author is using these possessive forms to describe priests whose work related to the care of the **sanctuary** and priests whose work related to offering sacrifices to **God**. If a speaker of your language would not use possessive forms in this way, you could express these ideas in another way. The UST models one way to do that.

Here, **face** represents “presence.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language, here and in verse 31. Alternate translation: [in the presence of]

Quote: בֵּֽית־אָ֣ב אֶחָ֗ד אָחֻז֙ לְ⁠אֶלְעָזָ֔ר וְ⁠אָחֻ֥ז ׀ אָחֻ֖ז לְ⁠אִיתָמָֽר
Note: The expression **and was taken, was taken** represents the standard written Hebrew text as we have it today. This reading, however, does not seem to make sense. Scholars have proposed that a scribe may have written the last consonant of a word incorrectly. With a different consonant, this would say “and one was taken,” which seems to fit the meaning of this passage better. The UST follows that interpretation. You may want to follow the major translation in your area. Alternate translation: [One house of a father was taken for Eleazar, and one was taken for Ithamar]

Quote: בֵּֽית־אָ֣ב אֶחָ֗ד אָחֻז֙ לְ⁠אֶלְעָזָ֔ר וְ⁠אָחֻ֥ז ׀ אָחֻ֖ז לְ⁠אִיתָמָֽר
Note: Since the author says in verse 5 that “they divided them by lots, these with these,” he does not seem to mean here that the officials alternately drew lots to give assignments to clans descended from Eleazar and clans descended from Ithamar. (That procedure would only have worked for eight rounds, after which eight clans from Eleazar would have remained without counterparts from Ithamar.) Instead, the author seems to be using an expression equivalent to “these with these”: **one … for Eleazar, and one … for Ithamar**. The idea seems to be that the assignment that went with a lot did not depend on which ancestor a clan had. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [The assignment that went with the lot did not depend on whether Eleazar or Ithamar was the ancestor of the clan whose name was drawn]

If your language would not represent a number in a form such as **first** or **second**, you could represent such numbers in a form that your language would use, here and through verse 18. Alternate translation: [lot number one … lot number two]

The author is using the adjective **second** as a noun to mean a certain kind of thing, a lot. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate such adjectives with equivalent phrases, here and through verse 18. Alternate translation: [the second lot]

The author is not referring to a specific **appointment**. He means the appointments of all 24 of these clans to serve in the temple on a rotating basis. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [These were their appointments]

Here, **hand** represents the agency of a person. See how you translated the similar expression in [11:3](../11/03.md). Alternate translation: [according to the regulation that Aaron their father had established]
The author is using the term **father** to mean “ancestor.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [their ancestor]

The author means that the **sons of Levi** or Levites whom he lists in verses 20–30 were **left** after the priests received their assignments. In other words, these are some of the Levites who were not priests. Since further Levites and their duties as singers, gatekeepers, and treasurers are described in chapters 25 and 26, it seems that the duty of the clans listed here was to assist the priests. Verse 31 seems to suggest this. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Some Levites who were not priests were assigned to assist the priests]

The author is not referring to a specific **Isharite**. He means the Isharites in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Of the Izharites]

The author is using the adjectives **second**, **third**, and **fourth** as nouns to mean certain kinds of people. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate these adjectives with equivalent phrases. Alternate translation: [son number two … son number three … son number four]
See how you translated the same expression in [23:32](../23/32.md). Alternate translation: [their kinsmen]

The author is referring to all of these Levite clans by naming two extremes, those descended from **fathers of the head** and those descended from a **youngest brother**. It seems that the expression **fathers of the head** is equivalent to **heads of fathers**, that is, heads of father’s houses or clans, and that it indicates an eldest brother who was a family leader. The idea is that the leaders did not take birth order, and thus family rank, into consideration in these assignments. This is another description of an impartial process, likes the ones in verses 5 and 6. The UST models one way to express this meaning in plain language.

The author is not referring to a specific **youngest brother**. He means the youngest brothers in all of the clans he has listed. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [their youngest brothers]

# 1 Chronicles 25 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues the final section the book, which describes how David established arrangements for the worship of the Israelites. It relates how David and the Israelite leaders assigned certain Levites to a rotating schedule of duty as temple musicians.

1. How David and the leaders assigned the Levite musicians to their schedule (1–6)
2. The schedule of duty for these Levites (7–19)

Here, **hand** and **hands** represent the control or direction of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly, here and in verses 3 and 6. Alternate translation: [under the direction of Asaph … under the supervision of the king]

The name “Shimei” appears after Jeshaiah in one Hebrew manuscript and in the ancient Greek translation. That makes sense, since Shimei is listed in v. 17 among the clan leaders who received assignments. It appears that his name has been accidentally omitted from the standard Hebrew text as we have it today. You may want to follow the alternative reading of the ancient Greek translation, or you may want to follow the major translation in your area. Alternate translation: [Gedaliah and Zeri and Jeshaiah and Shimei, Hashabiah and Mattithiah]

The author is using the term **words** to mean a promise that God spoke to Heman by using words. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in fulfillment of the promise of God]

The author is speaking as if Heman were an animal with a **horn** that God could **lift up**. An animal that lifts its horn is demonstrating strength and assertiveness. Accordingly, in this culture, a horn represented strength and dignity. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to make him strong] or [to give him dignity]
Here the word **For** introduces not a reason but an elaboration. Alternate translation: [Indeed,]

The author is speaking of the temple that the Israelites would build for Yahweh as if it were a **house** in which Yahweh would live. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the temple of Yahweh … the temple of God]
The author is using the term **brothers** to mean “relatives.” Alternate translation: [their kinsmen] or [their fellow Levites]

The expression **having been taught** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [who had learned]

The author is referring to all of the Levites he has listed by naming two extremes, **small** and **great**, and by describing two main positions that these musicians could be in, that of a **teacher** or that of a **student**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [no matter how important a man was and no matter how accomplished a musician he was]

If your language would not represent a number in a form such as **first** or **second**, you could represent such numbers in a form that your language would use, here and through verse 31. Alternate translation: [lot number one … lot number two]

The author is using the adjective **second** as a noun to mean a certain kind of thing, a lot. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate such adjectives with equivalent phrases, here and through verse 31. Alternate translation: [the second lot]

If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information that this first lot selected **Joseph** before the information that Joseph belonged to the family of **Asaph**. Alternate translation: [for Joseph son of Asaph]

The author must mean implicitly that 12 of Joseph’s brothers (relatives) and sons served with him. Otherwise, the list does not total 288, as verse 7 states. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [for Joseph, his sons and his brothers, 12]

The author makes clear in this instance that the expression “his sons and his brothers” in the rest of the chapter includes the named individual, so you do not need to indicate that in the following verses.

Since Gedaliah’s literal brothers are listed separately, it is clear that here the author is using the term **brothers** to mean other relatives who served with him. Alternate translation: [and his kinsmen]

The name **Izri** is a variant of the name “Zeri” in verse 3. Recall whether your translation team decided to use the same name for a given person in each instance where he appears or whether you decided to use the name that the biblical author does, even if that is a variant. Alternate translation: [for Zeri]

The name **Jesharelah** is a variant of the name “Asharelah” in verse 2. You may have decided to use the same name for a given person in each instance where he appears. Alternate translation: [Asharelah]
The name **Azarel** is a variant of the name “Uzziel” in verse r. You may have decided to use the same name for a given person in each instance where he appears. Alternate translation: [Uzziel]

# 1 Chronicles 26 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues the final section the book, which describes how David established arrangements for the worship of the Israelites. It relates how David and the Israelite leaders assigned certain Levites to a rotating schedule of duty as gatekeepers and treasurers.

1. Levite clans whose members were gatekeepers (1–19)
    1. Introduction (1a)
    2. Korahites, sons of Meshelemiah (1b–3, 9) and Obed Edom (4–8)
    3. Merarites, sons of Hosah (10–11)

    1. Introduction (20)
    2. Levites responsible for the treasuries of the house of God (21–24)
    3. Levites responsible for the treasuries dedicated items (25–28)
3. Levite clans whose members were officials and judges (29–32)

The author is using the adjectives **firstborn**, **second**, **third**, and **fourth** as nouns to mean certain kinds of people. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate these adjectives with equivalent phrases, here and in verses 3–5 and 10–11. Alternate translation: [the eldest son … son number two … son number three … son number four]
Here the word **for** introduces not a reason but an observation. Alternate translation: [indeed,]

The expression **were born** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And Shemaiah his son had sons]

Quote: הַ⁠מִּמְשָׁלִ֖ים לְ⁠בֵ֣ית אֲבִי⁠הֶ֑ם כִּֽי־גִבּ֥וֹרֵי חַ֖יִל הֵֽמָּה
Note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [and since they were warriors of valor, they were rulers in the house of their father]
See how you translated the expression “sons and brothers” in [25:10–31](../25/10.md). Alternate translation: [And sons and other relatives]
See how you translated the term “head” in [23:8](../23/08.md). Alternate translation: [the leader … the leader]
See how you translated the same expression in [24:4](../24/04.md). Alternate translation: [to the clan leaders]
The author is using the term **brothers** to mean “relatives.” Alternate translation: [their kinsmen] or [their fellow Levites]
See how you translated the same expression in [25:6](../25/06.md). Alternate translation: [in the temple of Yahweh]
See how you translated the similar expression in [25:8](../25/08.md). Alternate translation: [for each clan, without regard to how important it was]

The author is using **for gate and gate** as a common expression of his culture to mean “for each gate.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [for each gate] or [to assign the gates]

When the author says that this lot **fell to Shemeliah**, he is using a common expression of his culture to mean that when the leaders cast this lot, the result indicated Shemeliah. He does not mean that this lot literally fell onto Shemeliah. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And the eastward lot came up for Shelemiah] or [And the eastward lot selected Shelemiah]

The author is describing this lot as **eastward** to mean that it was the one that would assign the eastward gate of the temple courtyard to a group of Levites to guard. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language, hear and for the terms **northward** in this verse and “southward” in the next verse. Alternate translation: [the lot for the eastward gate]

The name **Shemeliah** is a variant of the name “Meshelemiah” in verse 1. Recall whether your translation team decided to use the same name for a given person in each instance where he appears or whether you decided to use the name that the biblical author does, even if that is a variant. Alternate translation: [to Meshelemiah]

Quote: וּ⁠זְכַרְיָ֨הוּ בְנ֜⁠וֹ יוֹעֵ֣ץ ׀ בְּ⁠שֶׂ֗כֶל הִפִּ֨ילוּ֙ גּֽוֹרָל֔וֹת וַ⁠יֵּצֵ֥א גוֹרָל֖⁠וֹ צָפֽוֹנָ⁠ה
Note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about which gate this lot selected before the information about who Zechariah was. Alternate translation: [And the lot for the northward gate, when they cast it, came out for Zechariah his son, who was a counselor with insight]

Quote: לְ⁠עֹבֵ֥ד אֱדֹ֖ם נֶ֑גְבָּ⁠ה וּ⁠לְ⁠בָנָ֖י⁠ו בֵּ֥ית הָ⁠אֲסֻפִּֽים
Note: The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [When the lot for Obed Edom came out, it indicated that he and his group would guard the southward gate, and when the lot for his sons came out, it indicated that they would guard the house of stores]

The author is using this possessive form to describe a **house** (that is, a building, an annex of the temple) that was characterized by being a place where **stores** (that is, supplies and equipment) were kept. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the storehouse]

Quote: לְ⁠שֻׁפִּ֤ים וּ⁠לְ⁠חֹסָה֙ לַֽ⁠מַּעֲרָ֔ב עִ֚ם שַׁ֣עַר שַׁלֶּ֔כֶת בַּֽ⁠מְסִלָּ֖ה הָ⁠עוֹלָ֑ה
Note: The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [When the lots for Shuppim and Hosah came out, they indicated that they and their groups would guard the western gate and the gate of Shallecheth on the ascending highway]

The author seems to be using this phrase to indicate that while these two gates were close together, each had its own guards. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [with each gate having its own guards]

The author is representing each of these gates by referring to from what direction a person would enter through them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [At the eastern gate … at the northern gate … at the southern gate]

It seems that **six Levites** were needed as gatekeepers at the eastern gate, as opposed to **four** at the other gates, because the eastern gate was the main entrance to the temple courtyard, and so it was the busiest. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [At the busy eastern gate]

In the ancient Greek translation, the phrase “to the day” follows this phrase, as in the rest of the verse. This seems to be the original reading. You may want to follow that reading, or you may want to follow the major translation in your area. Alternate translation: [six Levites to the day]

The author is using **to the day** as a common expression of his culture to mean “each day.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [per day … per day] or [each day … each day]

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [two at each of the two entrances]
See how you translated the similar expression in [6:33](../06/33.md). Alternate translation: [for the clan of the Korahites and for the clan of the Merarites]

# 1 Chronicles 28 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues the final section the book, which describes how David established arrangements for the worship of the Israelites. It relates how David summoned the Israelite leaders to Jerusalem to exhort them to support Solomon as their king and to remain loyal to Yahweh. It also describes how David exhorted Solomon to build the temple and the plans that David gave him for that project.

1. David summons the Israelite leaders to Jerusalem and addresses them (1–8)
2. The first part of David’s address to Solomon (9–10)
3. The author describes the plans that David gave to Solomon (11–18)
4. The rest of David’s address to Solomon (19–21)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Yahweh’s temple as his “footstool”

When David says in verse 2 that he wanted to build a temple “as a footstool of the feet of our God,” he is using an image that also occurs elsewhere in the Bible. This image envisions heaven as the place of God’s throne and the earth as the place of his footstool, so that God is present on earth as well as in heaven, although in a lesser sense. The psalmist says in [132:7](../132/007.md), for example, speaking of going to the temple, “Let us go to his dwellings; let us bow down at the footstool of his feet.”

### Why does the author speak in verse 16 of “tables” for the sacred bread?

[Leviticus 24:5–9](../lev/24/05.md) describes a single table in front of the lampstand in the tent of meeting for the bread of the arrangement. But according to [2 Chronicles 4:7–8](../2ch/04/07.md), when Solomon built the temple, he made ten lampstands and ten gold tables to put in front of them. [2 Chronicles 4:19](../2ch/04/19.md) says that the sacred bread was on these tables. But this was not a departure from what Yahweh wanted. This chapter indicates that it was part of the “plan” that the Spirit of Yahweh revealed to David.

# 1 Chronicles 29 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter concludes the final section the book, which describes how David established arrangements for the worship of the Israelites. It relates how David told the assembled Israelite leaders how much he had contributed for the temple from his personal wealth and how he challenged them to give as well. It describes their generous gifts, and it records the prayer of thanksgiving that David offered for them. It then relates how the Israelites celebrated together and how Solomon succeeded David as king. The chapter ends with a description of David’s death and a summary of his reign.

1. David describes his contributions and challenges the Israelites to give (1–5)
2. The Israelite leaders give generously (6–9)
3. David’s prayer of thanksgiving for the gifts (10–19)
4. The people worship Yahweh and celebrate together (20–22a)
5. Solomon succeeds David as king (22b–25)
6. Conclusion to the reign of David (26–30)

Note: David is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [But I and my people do not really have the power to offer freely like this.]
Here the word **For** introduces not a reason but an explanation. Alternate translation: [After all,]

Here, **hand** represents a person possessing something. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and what we have given to you already belonged to you]
Here the word **For** introduces not a reason but an elaboration. Alternate translation: [Indeed,]

David is using the expression **to your face ** to mean “in your presence.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [we are foreigners and settlers in your presence]

The terms **foreigners** and **settlers** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. They both referred to people from another country who were living in a land without the right to own property there. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [we are landless immigrants to your face]

David is speaking as if the Israelites were actually **foreigners** and **settlers** in their own land and as if Yahweh were a native of the land, in whose presence they were living. He means that it is as if they do not have any means of production, while Yahweh does. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [everything we have comes from you; we are not able to produce anything ourselves]

David is using the term **fathers** to mean “ancestors.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly, here and in verse 18. Alternate translation: [and the same was true of all of our ancestors]

The point of this comparison is that just as a **shadow** is fleeting, so are the **days** of a person’s life. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. The UST models one way to do that.

David does not mean that every person’s life is completely **without hope**. He means specifically that no person has the hope of continuing to live and never dying. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and without hope of not dying]
See how you translated the similar expression “the name of your glory” in [29:13](../29/13.md). Alternate translation: [for your holy name] or [for your holy reputation]
See how you translated the expression “from your hand” in [29:14](../29/14.md). Alternate translation: [it already belongs to you]
Here the **heart** represents a person’s motives and intentions. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [each person’s motives]

David is using the plural **uprightnesses** where he could have used the singular form. This suggests that he is using the plural form to emphasize the sincere quality of this attribute. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the singular and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [and are pleased with genuine uprightness]

The expression **are pleased** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and that genuine uprightness pleases you]
David is continuing to use the **heart** to represent a person’s motives and intentions. Alternate translation: [With genuinely upright intentions]

David is stating the pronoun **I** separately, even though the verb translated as **I have offered** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize his personal role in the activity he describes so that he can then refer to the complementary role of the **people**. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [For my part, I have offered freely]

David is using the demonstrative adjective **these** as a noun to mean the gifts he has given. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [all of these gifts]

Quote: וְ⁠עַתָּ֗ה עַמְּ⁠ךָ֙ הַ⁠נִּמְצְאוּ־פֹ֔ה רָאִ֥יתִי בְ⁠שִׂמְחָ֖ה לְ⁠הִֽתְנַדֶּב־לָֽ⁠ךְ
Note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put David’s observation that he sees **with rejoicing** at the start of this sentence. Alternate translation: [And now I see with rejoicing that your people found here have offered freely to you]
See how you translated the similar expression in [24:4](../24/04.md). Alternate translation: [your people who are here]

Quote: שֳׁמְרָ⁠ה־זֹּ֣את לְ⁠עוֹלָ֔ם לְ⁠יֵ֥צֶר מַחְשְׁב֖וֹת לְבַ֣ב עַמֶּ֑⁠ךָ
Note: Since, in this context, the **heart** represents a person’s thoughts, it might seem that also saying **intention** and **thoughts** would be to express extra information in a way that would not be natural in your language. If so, you can shorten this expression. Alternate translation: [make this something that your people forever intend]

In this instance, the **heart** represents a person’s feelings and commitments. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and establish their loyalty toward you] or [and establish them as loyal toward you]

David is once again using the **heart** to represent a person’s feelings and commitments. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a sincere commitment]

The terms **commandments**, **testimonies**, and **statutes** mean similar things. David is using the three terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation, as in the UST: [to obey all of your laws]

The phrases **to do everything** and **to build** together express a single idea. The phrase **do everything** tells in what way Solomon would **build** the temple. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. The UST models one way to do that.

The author is using **the morrow of that day** as a common expression of his culture to mean “the following morning.” He does not mean the morning of the same day when David addressed the assembly. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the following morning] or [on the morning of the next day]
If your language would not represent a number in a form such as **second**, you could represent this number in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [for time number two]

The author is using the adjective **second** as a noun to mean a certain thing, a time or occasion. (He is referring back to [23:1](../23/01.md), when David first “made Solomon his son reign.”) The ULT indicates this by supplying the word **time**. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [as they had done once before]

The author assumes that readers will understand that by **a leader**, he means Solomon, not some other person. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and they anointed him as a leader for Yahweh] or [and they anointed him as king of Yahweh’s people]

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and they anointed Zadok to be the high priest]

The author assumes that his readers will know that by **listened**, he means that the Israelites did what Solomon told them to do. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and all of the Israelites obeyed him]

Quote: וְ⁠כָל־הַ⁠שָּׂרִים֙ וְ⁠הַ⁠גִּבֹּרִ֔ים וְ⁠גַ֕ם כָּל־בְּנֵ֖י הַ⁠מֶּ֣לֶךְ דָּוִ֑יד נָ֣תְנוּ יָ֔ד תַּ֖חַת שְׁלֹמֹ֥ה הַ⁠מֶּֽלֶךְ
Note: The author is speaking as if these leaders had actually held Solomon up with their hands. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And all of the leaders and the warriors and also all of the sons of King David supported King Solomon] or [And all of the leaders and the warriors and also all of the sons of King David were loyal to King Solomon]
See how you translated the expression “to above” in [22:5](../22/05.md). Alternate translation: [very great]

The author is using the term **eyes** to mean “perspective,” “judgment,” or “opinion.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in the regard of all the Israelites]

The author is speaking as if the **majesty of a kingdom** were a garment that Yahweh could have **put on** Solomon. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And he made him a majestic king over Israel]

The author is using the expression **to the face of** to mean “before” or “previous to.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [such as no king before him had ever had]

Quote: וְ⁠הַ⁠יָּמִ֗ים אֲשֶׁ֤ר מָלַךְ֙ עַל־יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל אַרְבָּעִ֖ים שָׁנָ֑ה
Note: The author is using the term **days** to refer to a specific time, the time of David’s reign. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And the time that he reigned over Israel was 40 years]

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [for 33 years]

The phrases **in good old age** and **full of days** mean similar things. The author is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [when he was quite elderly]

The author assumes that readers will understand that he is using the term **good** to mean “considerable.” You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [when he was considerably old]

The author is speaking as if **days**, **wealth**, and **glory** were objects and as if David had been a container that was **full** of them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [having lived for many days and obtained much wealth and glory] or [having lived for a long time and obtained much wealth and glory]

Quote: וְ⁠דִבְרֵי֙ דָּוִ֣יד הַ⁠מֶּ֔לֶךְ הָ⁠רִאשֹׁנִ֖ים וְ⁠הָ⁠אֲחרֹנִ֑ים הִנָּ֣⁠ם כְּתוּבִ֗ים עַל־דִּבְרֵי֙ שְׁמוּאֵ֣ל הָ⁠רֹאֶ֔ה וְ⁠עַל־דִּבְרֵי֙ נָתָ֣ן הַ⁠נָּבִ֔יא וְ⁠עַל־דִּבְרֵ֖י גָּ֥ד הַ⁠חֹזֶֽה
Note: In this verse and the next verse, the author is using phrases that he will use regularly in 2 Chronicles, as he continues this story of Israel’s kings, to conclude the account of kings’ reigns. If you have already translated the books of 1 Kings and 2 Kings, see how you translated the similar conclusions to accounts of kings’ reigns. Alternate translation: [Now you can read about the matters of King David, the first and the last, in the records that Samuel the seer, Nathan the prophet, and Gad the visionary kept]

The author is referring to all of the **matters of King David** (that is, the events of his reign) by naming two extremes, **the first** events and **the last** events. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [events from his entire reign]

Quote: הִנָּ֣⁠ם כְּתוּבִ֗ים עַל־דִּבְרֵי֙ שְׁמוּאֵ֣ל הָ⁠רֹאֶ֔ה וְ⁠עַל־דִּבְרֵי֙ נָתָ֣ן הַ⁠נָּבִ֔יא וְ⁠עַל־דִּבְרֵ֖י גָּ֥ד הַ⁠חֹזֶֽה
Note: The author is using the term **words** to represent what these prophets recorded by using words. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [behold them, written in the records of Samuel the seer and in the records of Nathan the prophet and in the records of Gad the visionary]

Quote: הִנָּ֣⁠ם כְּתוּבִ֗ים עַל־דִּבְרֵי֙ שְׁמוּאֵ֣ל הָ⁠רֹאֶ֔ה וְ⁠עַל־דִּבְרֵי֙ נָתָ֣ן הַ⁠נָּבִ֔יא וְ⁠עַל־דִּבְרֵ֖י גָּ֥ד הַ⁠חֹזֶֽה
Note: The expression **written** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [behold, Samuel the seer, Nathan the prophet, and Gad the visionary have written about them in their records]

The author does not mean that the things he lists in this verse are in the records of the prophets in addition to the “matters of King David.” He means that these are some of the things that those records contain. If this would not be clear from the word **with**, you may want to use a different connecting word. Alternate translation: [including]

The words **reign** and **might** together express a single idea. The word **might** tells what characterized David’s **reign**. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [the many ways in which he reigned mightily]

Quote: וְ⁠הָ⁠עִתִּ֗ים אֲשֶׁ֨ר עָבְר֤וּ עָלָי⁠ו֙ וְ⁠עַל־יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל וְ⁠עַ֖ל כָּל־מַמְלְכ֥וֹת הָ⁠אֲרָצֽוֹת
Note: The author is using **the times that passed over** as a common expression of his culture to mean “the things that happened.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the events that involved him and the Israelites and the foreign kingdoms around them] or [and the things that happened to him and to Israel and to all of the kingdoms of the lands]
